title: Ramadan: breaking with a date
hookLine: at sunset, a date and water, and a du'a

lines: A LONG TABLE, A HUNDRED PEOPLE.
A FEW DATES ON EVERY PLATE.
cards: A long table in a mosque hall, paper cloths, plastic cups.

A hundred people sitting down, some who know each other, some who don't: a student far from home, a taxi driver on his break, an elderly couple, a neighbor who isn't Muslim but was invited. Nobody's eating.
Every plate has a few dates on it, and a cup of water. Everyone's watching the clock, or listening.
Then, from the front, the call to the sunset prayer begins, and a hundred hands reach, at the same moment, for one small date.

teach.b: It's called iftar, from a root meaning to break open, to split: the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, as maghrib comes in. The way it starts goes back to the Prophet ﷺ.

teach.h: FRESH DATES, DRIED DATES, OR WATER.
teach.b: A companion, Anas, said the Prophet would break his fast with fresh dates before praying; if there were none, with dried dates; if none, with a few sips of water. That's all. Not a feast first.
Something small and sweet, and water. The feast, if there is one, comes after. And there's a good kind of hurry to it.
A hadith in Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hasten to break the fast. The point isn't to linger and prove strength. When the sun's gone, the fast is done.
There's a short prayer reported for the moment, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: the thirst has gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills.
Three plain facts, said with a date still in your mouth. Then the line that makes it sweet.

In Bukhari, the Prophet said the fasting person has two joys: one when they break their fast, and one when they meet their Lord. The first is right there at the table. And the tradition prizes sharing it.
A hadith in Tirmidhi says whoever gives food to a fasting person to break their fast has the same reward as the one who fasted, without taking anything away from theirs.
That's why mosques set out those long tables, and why strangers get invited.

how: At sunset during Ramadan, Muslims break the fast promptly, often with dates and water, pray maghrib, and then eat the evening meal, frequently at communal iftars in mosques and homes.

o: the meal that breaks the fast at sunset
a lunch shared with friends at midday
the evening prayer said just after sunset

games.q: what's inside the iftar — tap the pairs.
p: from a root: to break open
breaking the fast, and meeting the Lord

the Prophet ﷺ broke his fast with a large meal first

games.q: the sun has set and the call to maghrib begins. you have no dates. what did the Prophet ﷺ do in that case?
o: wait until after the prayer to eat anything
take a few sips of water
eat the full meal right away
games.why: if there were no fresh or dried dates, he broke his fast with a few sips of water (Abu Dawud, from Anas).

practice: Before your next meal, even if your fast is only the hours since you last ate, sit down and take something small and sweet first, a date if you have one or a piece of fruit, and a glass of water.
Eat it slowly, noticing the first taste of sweetness and the water going down, and wait a moment before the rest. If you pray, you can say bismillah first.

wordCard.voice: Iftar. The meal that breaks the fast at sunset: a date, water, a few words, and the first of two joys. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: breaking the fast, from a root meaning to break open or split.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet at sunset. The first joy is one you can share. That's day one hundred twenty-two.
